chunks.text: Biotechnology lets scientists copy a single DNA molecule into billions, cut and paste genes between organisms, read the exact sequence of a genome, and precisely edit individual genes. It works by repurposing the cell's own DNA machinery as laboratory tools.

Two unifying facts make biotechnology possible: DNA's structure is universal (the same A-T, G-C base pairing in all organisms), and the genetic code is nearly universal (the same codons specify the same amino acids), so tools and genes transfer across species.
PCR (polymerase chain reaction) is DNA replication in a test tube, used to amplify a tiny DNA sample into billions of copies for diagnostics, forensics, and research.

PCR cycles through three temperature steps: denature (~95°C to separate the strands), anneal (cool so short primers bind the target sequence), and extend (heat-stable Taq polymerase builds new strands). Each cycle doubles the DNA, so ~30 cycles make over a billion copies.

Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size. Samples are loaded into wells and an electric current is applied; because DNA's phosphate backbone is negatively charged, all fragments migrate toward the positive electrode.
In a gel, smaller DNA fragments slip through the sieve-like gel easily and travel farther from the wells, while larger fragments are held back and stay near the wells. Farther = smaller.
Restriction enzymes are molecular scissors that cut DNA at specific recognition sequences. Many cut in a staggered way that leaves short single-stranded overhangs called sticky ends.
Cutting both a gene of interest and a plasmid with the same restriction enzyme gives them matching, complementary sticky ends, so the gene can base-pair with the opened plasmid.
DNA ligase (the same backbone-sealing enzyme used in replication) joins the gene and plasmid together, producing recombinant DNA — a plasmid carrying a gene from another organism.
A plasmid is a small circular DNA molecule used as a vector to carry genes into bacteria. Recombinant plasmids often include a selectable marker such as an antibiotic-resistance gene.

Transformation is the uptake of foreign DNA by bacteria. A selectable marker lets only successfully transformed cells survive on a selective plate, identifying which bacteria took up the recombinant plasmid.

Because the genetic code is universal, a transformed bacterium transcribes and translates the inserted gene to produce the desired protein. Multiplying bacteria become living factories that mass-produce human insulin, growth hormone, and clotting factors.

CRISPR-Cas9, borrowed from a bacterial antiviral immune system, uses a short guide RNA programmed to match a target DNA sequence; the guide leads the Cas9 protein to that exact site, where it cuts the DNA.

After CRISPR cuts, the cell's repair machinery either disables the gene or, if a template is supplied, pastes in a corrected sequence. Because the guide RNA can match almost any sequence, CRISPR is fast, cheap, and precise.
The first CRISPR therapy, for sickle-cell disease, was approved in 2023, showing how gene editing has moved from a research tool to an approved treatment in about a decade.

DNA sequencing reads the actual order of bases in DNA. The Human Genome Project first read all ~3 billion human base pairs over more than a decade; today a genome can be sequenced in about a day at a tiny fraction of the original cost.
Sequencing powers personalized medicine, the identification of disease genes, and evolutionary biology, since comparing genomes reveals how closely organisms are related (connecting to phylogeny).

DNA profiling (fingerprinting) uses the fact that individuals vary in the number of short tandem repeats in non-coding DNA. PCR amplifies these regions, electrophoresis separates them, and the resulting band pattern is as individual as a fingerprint.

To interpret a profiling gel, compare band positions between lanes: samples from the same person produce bands at the same positions. A suspect whose bands match the crime-scene bands at every position is a genetic match; one different band excludes a suspect.
Common biotechnology mix-ups: PCR copies DNA, sequencing reads its base order, and electrophoresis sorts by size — three different jobs. Restriction enzymes cut DNA while ligase joins it.
Recombinant DNA replaced insulin extracted from pig and cow pancreases with unlimited, identical-to-human insulin made by bacteria or yeast, eliminating scarcity and allergic reactions.

Genetically modified crops engineered for pest resistance, drought tolerance, or enhanced nutrition (such as vitamin-A 'golden rice') can raise yields and fight malnutrition, while raising debates about ecological effects, seed control, and labeling.

Editing somatic (body) cells affects only the treated patient, but editing germ-line cells (embryos, eggs, sperm) would change every descendant and the human gene pool. The 2018 announcement of gene-edited babies was condemned worldwide as unethical and reckless.
